findings.title: OptimizedCursorPaginator allows negative offsets, enabling unbounded/invalid queryset slicing
findings.body: When `enable_advanced_features` is set and `cursor.offset < 0`, the code slices `queryset[start_offset:stop]` with a negative start. Django QuerySets do not support negative indexing and raise `ValueError/AssertionError` ("Negative indexing is not supported"), so any user-supplied cursor with a negative offset on the audit-log endpoint causes a 500. The inline comments claiming "the underlying Django ORM properly handles negative slicing automatically" and "safe because permissions are checked at the queryset level" are factually wrong. There is also no validation rejecting negative offsets as other paginators do (`BadPaginationError("Pagination offset cannot be negative")`).

findings.title: Possible AttributeError on organization_context.member and anonymous users
findings.body: `organization_context.member.has_global_access` is evaluated unconditionally; `RpcUserOrganizationContext.member` is `None` for users who are not members of the organization (e.g. a superuser accessing another org), which raises `AttributeError` and returns a 500 for every GET request in that case. Also `request.user.is_superuser` is accessed before confirming the user is authenticated. The check should be short-circuited/guarded (e.g. `getattr(organization_context.member, 'has_global_access', False)`).

findings.title: Undocumented query flag switches paginator and breaks cursor semantics for audit logs
findings.body: `optimized_pagination=true` swaps `DateTimePaginator` for `OptimizedCursorPaginator`, whose `get_item_key`/`value_from_cursor` treat the ordering key as a numeric value, not a datetime. Ordering is by `-datetime`, so `int(math.floor(value))` on a `datetime` raises `TypeError`, and cursors issued by one paginator are not interpretable by the other. This path appears untested and will 500 as soon as it is exercised.

findings.title: BasePaginator offset clamping changes pagination behavior inconsistently
findings.body: `start_offset = max(0, offset) if not cursor.is_prev else offset` clamps forward offsets to 0 but leaves prev-cursor offsets unclamped, so a negative offset on a prev cursor still reaches the queryset slice and crashes. Additionally the later check `elif len(results) == offset + limit + extra` still uses the unclamped `offset`, so when clamping occurred the extra-row trimming is computed against the wrong expected length and an extra row may be returned on a page.

findings.title: Span eviction limit hardcoded to 1000 and silently drops spans, ignoring max_segment_spans config
findings.body: The eviction threshold `1000` is hardcoded in Lua while `SpansBuffer.max_segment_spans` (default 1001) is now unused in Python, so the configured limit has no effect and the two can diverge. More importantly `zpopmin` removes the spans with the lowest `end_timestamp_precise`, silently discarding span data from oversized segments without any metric/log (the previous code incremented `spans.buffer.flush_segments.segment_span_count_exceeded` and skipped the segment). Oversized segments will now be emitted partially, and the dropped span may be the root/segment span, producing a segment with the wrong `is_segment` marking.

findings.title: span_count can be stale/incorrect when both unions execute
findings.body: `span_count` is assigned from the first `zunionstore` and then possibly overwritten by the second, which is fine, but if only the first union runs and the parent merge is skipped, `span_count` reflects the cardinality *before* the current span's own zadd in some orderings; and if neither union runs `zcard` is queried. The net effect is that when a union happened, the count used for the `> 1000` eviction check can be lower than the actual set size (the new span payload is added by a separate pipeline step), so segments can exceed the intended cap or evict the wrong amount. Prefer always calling `zcard set_key` right before the eviction check.

findings.title: Redirect-chain limit silently reduced from 10000 to 1000, removing explanatory comment
findings.body: The loop bound was lowered from 10000 to 1000 and the comment documenting the consequence ("segment trees of depth 10k may not be joined together correctly") was deleted. Traces with redirect chains deeper than 1000 will now fail to be joined into a single segment, producing split segments, and the behavioral trade-off is no longer documented anywhere.

findings.title: max_segment_spans is now dead config and missing from __reduce__
findings.body: The span-count guard in `_load_segment_data` was removed, so `max_segment_spans` is no longer used anywhere; callers configuring it get no effect. Relatedly `__reduce__` still only passes `assigned_shards`, the two timeouts and `redis_ttl`, so `segment_page_size`, `max_segment_bytes` and `max_segment_spans` are reset to defaults when the buffer is pickled for multiprocessing — any non-default tuning is silently lost in the multiprocess consumer path.

findings.title: No test for the new in-insert eviction behavior
findings.body: The PR's headline change (zset-based buffer with eviction of the oldest spans once a segment exceeds 1000 spans) has no test. Tests were only mechanically updated with `end_timestamp_precise`. A test asserting that a segment with >1000 spans keeps the newest 1000 (and what happens to the root span) is needed, since this path silently drops customer data if it misbehaves.
